User: How many new cells does a tree lay down in a season?
Joe: A healthy tree in good soil can lay down a layer of new wood a few millimetres thick in a season, which works out to millions of cells. Each one of those cells laid down in spring stays fixed in the trunk for the rest of the tree's life.

User: What is a fibre cap on a hardwood trunk?
Joe: A fibre cap is the band of tough, non-conducting fibres that closes off the latewood at the end of each growth ring. In many ring-porous hardwoods it acts like a barrier that partly isolates the next ring from the one below it.

User: What is the difference between radial and tangential shrinkage?
Joe: Radial shrinkage is the loss across the grain from bark to pith, and it is the largest of the three. Tangential shrinkage runs around the circumference and is a little smaller, while longitudinal shrinkage along the stem is almost negligible.

User: What causes the honeycomb checking in a log end?
Joe: Honeycomb checking opens up as radial splits that meet the tangential ones, leaving a pattern like the inside of a honeycomb. It happens when the outside of the log dries and shrinks faster than the still-wet core, so the two pull apart.

User: What is casehardening in a drying kiln?
Joe: Casehardening happens when a log surface sets hard in the kiln before the centre has dried at all. The dry shell then holds the wet core under tension, and the board will crack the moment that tension is released at the planer.

User: What is the fascicular cambium?
Joe: The fascicular cambium is the strip of dividing cells that already sits inside each vascular bundle of a young stem, between its xylem and phloem. Once the bundle opens out and those bundles come round into a ring, the fascicular cambium is completed by the interfascicular cambium.

User: What happens to a stem that never forms the interfascicular cambium?
Joe: A stem that cannot close the ring stays unable to make secondary xylem, so it never gets thicker in the normal way. That is why monocot stems, and the anomalous wood of some tropical families, have a completely different internal plan.

User: How does a tree carry sugar from leaves to roots in winter?
Joe: Sugars leave the leaves in the phloem as they are remobilised in autumn, and pressure flow pushes them down toward the roots. The sink tissue draws sugar out of the sieve tubes, which keeps water moving in and keeps the pressure gradient going.

User: Does sap go up and down in the same tubes?
Joe: No, water and sugar travel in separate tissue systems even though they share the same trunk. Water moves upward through the xylem, and sugar moves both up and down through the phloem depending on where the source and the sink are.

User: What is the pressure flow idea in phloem transport?
Joe: Pressure flow holds that sugar loading at a source lowers the water potential of the phloem, so water enters from the xylem and raises the pressure. Sugar unloading at a sink drops that pressure again, and the gradient between the two ends moves the sap.

User: Why does girdling a branch kill the part above it?
Joe: A girdle removes the phloem all the way round, so the sugars made in the leaves above can no longer move down or sideways. The roots are cut off from their food supply, and after that the whole tree starves, not just the top.

User: How does a leaf vein differ from a root trace?
Joe: Leaf veins are bundles of xylem and phloem enclosed in a sheath and running through the lamina of the leaf. Roots have no such conducting bundles in their tips; instead their absorbing surface is a single layer of epidermis with root hairs behind it.

User: What is a leaf trace and where does it start?
Joe: A leaf trace is the strand of vascular tissue that leaves the stem to supply one leaf. It branches off from the vascular system just below a node, and the gap left in the cylinder of wood above it is one of the useful characters for reading a winter twig.

User: What is a leaf scar and what does its shape tell you?
Joe: A leaf scar is the mark left where a leaf's petiole detached from the twig. Its outline, the number of bundle scars inside it and the shape of the scars above and below it are all diagnostic characters for identifying a tree in winter.

User: What are stipules and why do they help in identification?
Joe: Stipules are small leaflike organs that sit at the base of a petiole, one on each side, before the leaf unfolds. In maples they form a pair of wings, and in the rose family they wrap the bud, so their fate is a strong field character.

User: What is a stipule scar?
Joe: A stipule scar is the small mark left beside a leaf scar where a stipule used to be attached. It sits inside the curve of the leaf scar rather than above it, and its position helps separate families that otherwise look alike on bare twigs.

User: How does a bundle scar form?
Joe: A bundle scar is the small dot left where the xylem and phloem of a leaf trace were severed. Its number inside the leaf scar tells you how the leaf was wired, and in some families that count is a reliable family character.

User: What is a node on a twig?
Joe: A node is the point on a twig where leaves, buds or branches were attached. Nodes are swollen slightly because a larger number of cells was produced there, and the pattern they leave above and below the leaf scar is what you read when the tree is bare.

User: What is the difference between a vascular bundle and a vascular strand?
Joe: In a stem the xylem and phloem travel together as a bundle, so the two terms are used interchangeably in most field guides. Where a leaf vein or a root trace is being described, strand is the more usual word because the tissue splits apart along its length.

User: Why does a cut branch on a birch bleed so much sap?
Joe: Birch sap sits under pressure in the xylem in spring, driven by root pressure rather than by the leaves. Cutting the stem opens the conduits and the pressure pushes the watery sap straight out, which is the basis of the birch sap tapping season.

User: What is sapwood in a conifer?
Joe: In a conifer the sapwood is the outer band of wood whose cells still conduct water, and it is usually pale and soft. Behind it the heartwood turns dark as resins and tannins accumulate, and its transport cells are already dead.

User: How many years of wood does a conifer keep as sapwood?
Joe: A conifer gradually converts sapwood to heartwood from the inside out, so only a band a few centimetres deep stays functional. In some species that band stays wide for a century, and in others the transition starts early and the living wood stays thin.

User: What is the dry heartwood of a cedar like?
Joe: Cedar heartwood is naturally durable because it carries extractives that discourage decay fungi. That is why western red cedar has been used for outdoor cladding for over a century without any preservative treatment at all.

User: Why does cedar shake resist decay better than pine?
Joe: Cedar heartwood is packed with phenolic extractives that act as a built-in fungicide, and its earlywood cells are narrow and thick walled. Pine heartwood carries far fewer extractives, so a cedar shake outlasts a pine board of the same thickness in wet weather.

User: What is the dark line in the wood right under a scar on a birch?
Joe: That dark line is a stain of phenolic extractives that ran into the wood as the sap bled from the wound. Birch bark is full of those compounds, and once they soak in they mark the cut permanently, which is why old peeling bark scars stay visible.

User: What makes the wood of a black walnut turn dark with age?
Joe: Black walnut heartwood darkens as its juglone-related extractives oxidise after the tree is cut. Freshly sawn walnut is a pale chocolate brown and it darkens noticeably over the following years as it cures.

User: What is a wood cell that has filled with resin called?
Joe: A resin duct that has been plugged by hardened resin is simply an occluded duct. In a fire-exposed pine the resin melts and runs, and once cooled it seals the duct so that beetles can no longer use it as an entry route.

User: Why does a burl form a swirled pattern inside?
Joe: A burl grows when dormant buds on the trunk start producing shoots without an orderly bud cycle. Each shoot drags a twisted stream of cells with it, and those irregular grain trails are what give burl its famous swirling figure.

User: What is included bark and why does it matter at cell level?
Joe: Included bark is bark tissue trapped inside the wood when two branches grow together, so it is living tissue buried in dead wood. It is a weak seam that never heals properly, which is why it is checked at every branch union on a structurally important tree.

User: How does a branch callus close a pruning wound?
Joe: The wound is closed by callus tissue rolling in from the sides, produced by the cambium around the wound edge. The roll-over is visible as a raised lip, and it is why a pruned stub leaves a permanent ring of scar tissue on the trunk.

User: Why does a large wound never heal completely in the middle?
Joe: Callus grows only from the edges, and it closes across the top of the wound rather than filling the whole exposed area. The wood behind the lip seals against decay but the interior of a big cut stays dead wood for the life of the tree.

User: What does a trunk section show about bark thickness?
Joe: A cross-section of a trunk shows a thin living band at the outside and a thick mass of dead bark behind it. Each time the outer bark falls off, the cork cambium lays down a fresh layer inside, so old trunks carry many stacked generations of periderm.

User: What is a periderm?
Joe: A periderm is the protective bark system made of a cork cambium, the cork cells it produces and a layer of living phloem inside that. It replaces the original epidermis once the stem starts to thicken, and it is what keeps water out of the living tissue.

User: Why does outer bark shed in plates?
Joe: Deep cracks and loose plates form where successive periderms cut off the dead outer tissue in irregular shapes. Weather then widens the cracks, so sycamores and pines end up shedding large flakes rather than smooth, continuous sheets.

User: What is a rhytidome?
Joe: A rhytidome is the thick, flaky outer bark made of several stacked dead periderms. It forms on old trunks and old roots, and because the dead layers are brittle it is where fire, sunscald and mechanical damage usually start.

User: What is a lenticel at the cell level?
Joe: A lenticel is a loose plug of corky cells that interrupts the periderm so gas can pass through the bark. The cells in the plug are spaced loosely rather than tightly, which is the same trick a leaf stoma uses to let air in.

User: Why do young twigs have bigger lenticels than old trunks?
Joe: A young twig is still breathing through its epidermis, so its lenticels are prominent and pale against the smooth bark. As the periderm thickens the lenticels become smaller and more scattered, and on an old trunk they are barely visible.

User: What happens to the vascular system inside an old heartwood log?
Joe: The conducting cells in the heartwood are dead, and their pits and vessels are blocked with gums, resins and tyloses. Water no longer moves there at all, so a hollow or decayed heartwood centre is not the same as a dead sapwood strip just under the bark.

User: How do trees with hollow trunks keep moving water?
Joe: The water conducting wood is the outer sapwood band, which is intact even when the centre has rotted away. As long as the sapwood ring stays wide enough to carry the crown, the tree can live with a hollow trunk for many more decades.

User: What is a spiral grain and how does it form?
Joe: A spiral grain is a twist in the fibre direction that runs at a slight angle up the trunk instead of straight. It happens when the fibres follow the direction of the spiral the tree laid down in its youth, and it shows as a diagonal figure on a sawn face.

User: What is the difference between radial and diagonal grain on a board?
Joe: Radial grain means the growth rings meet the face of the board at right angles, which happens on a perfect quarter sawn cut. Diagonal grain means the rings run across the board at an angle, so the grain lines and the ring lines cross on the surface.

User: What makes a board cup instead of warp?
Joe: Cupping is a curved bend across the width of a wide board as it dries. Tangential shrinkage is greater than radial, so the outside of each ring shrinks more than the inside and the board curls toward the bark side.

User: What is checking and how does it differ from splitting?
Joe: Checking is a set of fine cracks that open as a log dries from the outside in. Splitting is a single wide break that follows the grain, and both come from the outside of a log shrinking faster than the wet core inside it.

User: What does a wind-shaken tree look like in cross section?
Joe: A wind-shaken trunk shows rings that are crushed or pulled apart on the side that faced the prevailing wind. The wood fibres there are shredded even though the tree keeps growing, which is the record of storms it survived without toppling.

User: What is compression wood and what makes it?
Joe: Compression wood is reaction wood formed on the underside of a leaning conifer trunk or branch. Its cells are shorter, thicker walled and lignified differently, so it pushes rather than pulls, and it is denser than the normal wood around it.

User: What is tension wood in hardwoods?
Joe: Tension wood is reaction wood formed on the upper side of a leaning hardwood branch or trunk. It stretches in place as the tree straightens the lean, and because of its unusual cellulose it often shows as a pale, fuzzy patch on a planed face.

User: How does a tree know which side to put reaction wood?
Joe: The response is driven by gravity acting on the crown rather than by any deliberate sense of direction. Where the bending stress is greatest, the cambium changes the way it builds cells and lays down reaction wood on the correct side.

User: What is gelatinous fibre and where does it appear?
Joe: A gelatinous fibre is a tension wood fibre whose inner wall layer grows out into the cell lumen as a loose gel-like sheet. In hardwood tension wood it makes up much of the extra tissue and is mostly cellulose, which is why the wood swells oddly when it is cut.

User: How does a wound callus differ from an adventitious bud?
Joe: A wound callus is undifferentiated tissue that rolls in from an existing wound margin. An adventitious bud is a new organised shoot that arises on old wood or on a root where no bud was ever present, which is why epicormic shoots appear on stressed trunks.

User: Where do epicormic shoots come from on an old trunk?
Joe: Epicormic shoots grow from buds buried under the bark long ago, which are released when the trunk is damaged, girdled or suddenly exposed to light. They are often a stress response, so a heavy flush of them often signals that the crown is in trouble.

User: What is the difference between a burl and a crown gall?
Joe: A burl is a swelling of normal wood in which the grain has been dragged into swirls by irregular bud activity. A crown gall is a tumour-like mass of undifferentiated cells caused by a bacterium, and it forms at the root crown rather than in the trunk wood.

User: Why does the wood inside a knot run at an angle?
Joe: A knot is a branch base that was overgrown by the trunk, so the wood around it was laid down as the branch pushed out. The grain bends around the knot to accommodate it, which is why the fibres run diagonally and the wood is weaker there.

User: What is a nail plate used for in an old trunk?
Joe: A nail plate is a band of steel or aluminium driven into the wood just behind a wound to hold the bark and wood together. It stops the bark from splitting along the wound edge while the callus rolls in, and it is removed once the wound has closed.

User: What is a cavity in the heartwood called when it reaches the surface?
Joe: A cavity is simply the void left when heartwood has rotted out; when it opens to the outside it becomes a hollow. The rim of the hollow usually shows callus growth, which is the tree trying to wall the decay off from the living sapwood.

User: What keeps a wound from becoming a cavity?
Joe: The living tissue at the wound margin reacts to the injury and lays down barrier wood behind the callus. If that response stays ahead of the decay fungi, the damage stays confined to dead wood and never reaches the sapwood.

User: How does a tree seal off a pruning cut with wound wood?
Joe: The callus rolls over the cut and then a new periderm forms across the sealed surface underneath. Each year's periderm cut off adds another thin dead layer, so an old pruning cut ends up as a small pad of scar tissue in the grain.

User: What is a girdling root at the cell level?
Joe: A girdling root is a root that has grown across the trunk base and cut through the phloem on one side of the stem. Sugars made in the crown cannot pass that point, so the tissue above the cut starves even though the xylem still carries water.

User: What is the effect of a shallow root plate on wind stability?
Joe: A shallow plate gives a tall tree a low centre of gravity but poor leverage in a horizontal push. The overturning moment is resisted by the roots in the direction of the push, so a tree with a wide plate tips rather than snapping at the base.

User: How does buttress root form?
Joe: Buttresses develop where the trunk needs extra support against toppling, usually in trees on wet or shallow soils. The cambium lays down wide planks of sloping wood at the base, and they widen and deepen as the tree grows taller.

User: What is a knee and why do swamp trees make them?
Joe: A knee is a woody projection of the root crown above the mud surface in wetland trees. Bald cypress makes them prominently, and they carry extra root tissue up into the air where oxygen is available, though their exact function is still argued over.

User: How do the stilt roots of a mangrove work?
Joe: Stilt roots arc out of the trunk into the mud and brace the tree against waves and tides. They also hold the plant above waterlogged soil where roots could not otherwise breathe, and they trap sediment that builds up a new root bed.

User: What do aerial roots in a fig do?
Joe: Aerial roots on a fig grow downward from the branches and thicken into props once they reach the ground. They widen the tree's base, support heavy limbs, and add rooting area so the fig can spread into a small grove around its parent trunk.

User: What is a prop root in a banyan?
Joe: A prop root is a lateral root from the trunk or a branch that turns downward and becomes a stem-like support. As it thickens it carries its own leaves, so a single banyan trunk gradually becomes a many-trunked colony.

User: How do root hairs form?
Joe: Root hairs are single-cell extensions of the epidermis just behind the root tip, and each one is a separate cell. They are produced in a band behind the elongation zone and are short lived, so the absorbing surface is constantly renewed as the root grows.

User: What is the root cap for?
Joe: The root cap is a loose sleeve of cells at the very tip that wears away as the root pushes through soil. It protects the delicate division zone behind it and senses gravity and moisture, which is how the growing tip knows which way to turn.

User: How do roots detect a dry patch of soil?
Joe: Roots sense the gradient in soil moisture rather than any single value, so they proliferate where the soil is wetter. That is why a tree irrigating a small area of lawn grows a dense mat of roots in exactly that circle instead of spreading evenly.

User: What is the exodermis on a root?
Joe: The exodermis is the outer layer just inside the root epidermis, and it becomes suberised as the root matures. It limits water loss from the root and controls how much of the soil water can enter the conducting core once the tip has gone past its absorbing stage.

User: How do older roots behave differently from young roots?
Joe: A young root tip is the only part that absorbs water efficiently, and the root system grows new tips constantly. Older roots turn suberised and conductive but not absorbing, so the tree depends on replacing those absorbing tips rather than on deepening the old ones.

User: What is a haustorium in a parasitic plant?
Joe: A haustorium is the penetrating organ a parasite uses to tap into the vascular tissue of its host. It grows through the host cortex to the xylem and phloem, and once established the parasite draws both water and sugar from the host's circulation.

User: How does mistletoe tap into a host tree?
Joe: Mistletoe sends a haustorium from its own root into the host branch. The connection reaches the xylem for water but in most species it also forms a direct bridge to the host phloem, so the parasite takes sugars that the host had already made.

User: Why does mistletoe grow so high in a tree?
Joe: Mistletoe seeds are carried up by birds and land in the outer canopy where there is light. Seedlings that establish in shaded interior branches starve, so the parasite survives mostly in the sunny crown where its own leaves can pay for itself.

User: What is a phyllomorph in a eucalyptus?
Joe: A phyllomorph is a stage where a eucalyptus leaf and its stalk fuse into one flattened green structure that does the work of both. Shedding and regrowing these keeps the tree's photosynthetic surface young, and the old units fall away as bark-like debris.

User: What is a cladode and what does it do in a tree?
Joe: A cladode is a flattened stem segment that has taken over the job of a leaf. In some drought-adapted trees the true leaves are tiny or missing, and the green stem tissue carries the stomata and does the photosynthesis instead.

User: What does a liana gain by growing as a vine?
Joe: A liana puts almost no energy into making a self-supporting trunk and spends it on long, fast, thin stems. That lets it reach the canopy light quickly and spread across several trees, while its own narrow stem stays cheap to build.

User: How does a liana get water to the top of a tall host?
Joe: Some lianas solve the height problem by splitting their xylem at times of high demand, then sealing the breaks again. Others rely on very wide, easily refilled vessels, so a liana stem can move more water than a comparable diameter of host trunk.

User: What is the water reservoir inside a baobab trunk?
Joe: The baobab trunk is filled with soft, spongy wood that stores water for the dry season. It swells visibly after rain and shrinks during the long drought, so the trunk itself works as a seasonal buffer against a climate with almost no rain for months.

User: How do bottle trees store water?
Joe: Bottle-shaped trunks hold water in spongy wood rather than in a hollow cavity. Brachychiton, bottlebrush and other Australian forms swell after rain and contract during drought, using the reserve to keep leaves alive through dry spells.

User: What is a deciduous tropical tree's advantage over an evergreen one?
Joe: Dropping its leaves lets a tropical tree avoid losing water through transpiration at the worst time of year. It grows fast in the wet season on full light and shuts down through the dry season, which is the opposite strategy of an evergreen rainforest tree.

User: Why do evergreen tropical trees keep their leaves?
Joe: In a warm, moist rainforest there is no cold season and no dry season severe enough to pay for a bare period. Keeping leaves year round lets the tree use every good day, and it dominates nutrient-poor tropical soils where building new leaves constantly would be expensive.

User: What is water potential in a tree?
Joe: Water potential is the chemical energy of water in a plant, and the tree moves water from high potential to low. Soil, root, stem and leaf each sit at a different value, and the whole gradient from soil to leaf is what drives the flow.

User: How does water potential change from soil to leaf?
Joe: It falls steadily along the path. Soil water sits highest, then the root, then the stem, and the leaf sits lowest because evaporation from the stomata pulls on it, so the gradient always points upward.

User: What is predawn water potential used for?
Joe: Predawn water potential is measured just before sunrise, when the tree has finished transpiring for the night. At that moment stem water potential has relaxed back to match the soil, so the reading tells you how wet the soil actually is.

User: Why is midday water potential lower than predawn?
Joe: Through the day transpiration pulls hard on the xylem, so stem water potential drops until evening. The gap between the two readings is a direct measure of how hard the tree is working and how close it is to a water deficit.

User: What does a large drop in midday water potential suggest?
Joe: A large drop means the tree is drawing hard on its stored water reserves. When the stomata start to close to protect the leaf, that shows the tree has run out of the easy water and is running into genuine drought stress.

User: What is root pressure?
Joe: Root pressure is the positive pressure the root builds by actively pumping ions into the xylem. Water follows osmotically, and the pressure shows up as guttation and as the sap that runs from a cut stem of birch or maple in spring.

User: What is guttation and when does it happen?
Joe: Guttation is the appearance of water droplets at the edges of a leaf rather than a spray from the middle. It happens at night or early morning when the soil is wet, root pressure pushes water up, and there is no transpiration to carry it away as vapour.

User: Why is guttation not the same as dew?
Joe: Dew is atmospheric moisture condensing on a cold surface from the outside. Guttation is liquid water pushed up from inside the plant and out through hydathodes at the leaf margin, so the droplets sit at the tips and edges.

User: Can guttation damage a leaf?
Joe: Yes, if it happens every night the droplets sit on the blade until they evaporate and the salts in them concentrate. That scorch shows up first on the leaf margin, and it is a common sign of overwatering or poor drainage.

User: What is a hydathode?
Joe: A hydathode is a pore at the leaf tip or margin that releases liquid water rather than vapour. These pores never fully close, so they are a route for water out of the plant even when the stomata are shut during a drought.

User: What is cavitation in a tree?
Joe: Cavitation is the failure of a water-filled xylem conduit, which then fills with vapour instead of water. Once that happens the conduit stops conducting, and in a freeze or a severe drought the tree loses a fraction of its hydraulic capacity all at once.

User: What causes embolism in a winter tree?
Joe: Ice formation in the conduits pushes the dissolved gases out of solution, and those gas bubbles block the pathway once the ice thaws. Conifers with small tracheids are better protected because their pits close and hold the bubbles in place.

User: How do conifers resist winter embolism better than broadleaves?
Joe: Conifer tracheids are small in diameter and connect through pits with a sealing membrane. Broadleaf vessels are wide and connected by open perforation plates, so a single freeze can bubble the whole vessel and stop it completely.

User: What is pit aspiration in a drought-stressed tree?
Joe: Pit aspiration happens when a gas bubble is pulled through a pit membrane and seats against the sealing border. That closes the pit for good, so the tree trades conductivity for safety as the soil dries and the tension in the xylem climbs.

User: How does a tree recover from embolism?
Joe: Small conduits can refill because root pressure pushes new water into them and the tension is relieved overnight. Large vessels are far harder to refill, so a tree that has lost many large vessels during a drought may not fully recover that conducting capacity.

User: What is a hydraulic safety margin?
Joe: A hydraulic safety margin is the gap between the water potential at which stomata close and the level at which the conduits start to fail. A wide margin means the tree closes its stomata and holds on to its plumbing; a narrow one means it runs out of room.

User: What is the cavitation catastrophe theory?
Joe: It proposes that a tree has evolved to stay just above the point where its conduits would fail. Stomata respond well before that threshold is reached, so in practice embolism happens after the tree has already begun defending itself.

User: What is a stomatal conductance?
Joe: Stomatal conductance is how fast water vapour moves out through the stomata, and it is a measure of how open they are. It responds to light, carbon dioxide, temperature and soil moisture, and it rises through the morning and falls through the afternoon.

User: What is the midday depression in stomatal conductance?
Joe: It is the normal drop in stomatal opening around midday, driven by the leaf losing water faster than the soil can supply it. Closing down cuts that loss, and the same response shows up as wilting when the deficit becomes severe.

User: What is leaf water potential?
Joe: Leaf water potential is the tightest link in the chain, because the leaf is where water finally leaves as vapour. It is the most negative value in the plant, and it sets the suction that pulls the whole column up from the soil.

User: What is the difference between a wet tree and a turgid tree?
Joe: A turgid cell is one with enough internal water pressure to push firmly against its wall, which keeps the leaf firm. A cell that has lost water is flaccid instead, and a flaccid leaf droops, which is the everyday sign of wilting.

User: Why do tree trunks shrink and swell with water?
Joe: Living bark cells expand when they take up water and contract when they lose it, so the circumference of a large trunk changes measurably over a day. The change is driven by the sap underneath, so the best time to measure a trunk is at dawn before transpiration begins.

User: What is a dendrometer measuring?
Joe: A dendrometer measures the tiny change in stem circumference that comes from water movement in the sap. Over a day it traces the cycle of water stress, and over months it grows dense enough to show the annual increment in wood.

User: How does a tree handle the pull of a bigger crown?
Joe: Crown ratio is the link between canopy demand and the sapwood available to supply it. A tree with a large crown and little sapwood runs a very small safety margin, which is why arborists watch it closely after a crown is cut back.

User: What does a drought-induced hydraulic failure look like?
Joe: Leaves scorch from the tips inward, branch tips die back first, and the dieback starts on the side of the crown with the least access to water. In species that are not isohydric the stomata stay open longer and the leaf damage comes sooner.

User: What does an isohydric tree do during drought?
Joe: An isohydric species closes its stomata early and hard, sacrificing carbon gain to protect its plumbing. It keeps its hydraulic safety margin wide and shows less leaf damage, but it also stops growing and photosynthesising earlier in the drought.

User: What is the embolism repair mechanism in oaks?
Joe: Oaks can generate root pressure overnight in some soils and use it to push water back into large embolised vessels. That is part of why oaks recover from drought damage better than many other genera, even though they suffer the same embolism during the event.

User: How much water does a tree move on a hot day?
Joe: A large mature broadleaf tree in summer can move hundreds of litres across in a day through transpiration. The number varies hugely with species, size and weather, but it is the reason one big tree can change the humidity of a whole garden.

User: What is transpiration stream?
Joe: The transpiration stream is the continuous column of water drawn up through the xylem by leaf evaporation. It is the same column from root to crown, so a single cut at the base will stop water reaching every leaf above it.

User: How does the cohesion tension theory explain upward water movement?
Joe: Evaporation from a mesophyll cell creates a curved water surface in its pore, and surface tension pulls on the column behind it. Because water molecules cohere to each other, the tension is transmitted all the way down to the roots, and that pull is what lifts the sap.

User: What is capillary rise in a small trunk?
Joe: Capillary rise is water climbing a tube simply because the tube is narrower than the water's surface tension can hold. In seedlings it moves water a few centimetres, but it is far too weak to lift sap to the top of a mature tree.

User: How does root water uptake change with soil depth?
Joe: Uptake follows the depth where the soil is both moist and aerated, and in most soils that means the upper and middle layers. Only in dry summers do deep roots carry much of the load, and they are also the roots that die back first when the soil stays saturated.

User: Why do trees die from too much water as well as too little?
Joe: Waterlogged soil drives oxygen out of the pore space, and the roots stop taking up water even though it is everywhere. The tree then suffers a water deficit it cannot fix, so the symptoms look like drought while the ground is wet.

User: What is anoxia in tree roots?
Joe: Anoxia is the state of being starved of oxygen, which is what a root experiences in saturated soil. Without oxygen the root cannot respire efficiently, active uptake stops, and fine roots begin to die within days.

User: How quickly do roots suffocate in flooded soil?
Joe: Fine roots in saturated soil begin to lose function within days and are largely dead within a couple of weeks. Trees with adaptations such as knees, buttressed bases or surface roots handle it, and there are species that actively send oxygen to their submerged roots.

User: How does a mangrove send oxygen to its roots?
Joe: Some mangroves grow hollow aerial roots that vent directly to the air, so oxygen diffuses down into the buried root system. Others push oxygen out of the root surface as bubbles, which is why mud under a mangrove forest is often aerated.

User: What is the role of leaf temperature in water loss?
Joe: A warmer leaf drives transpiration faster because the air inside the leaf holds more vapour. Leaves also cool themselves by evaporating water, which is why a transpiring tree stays cooler in the sun than a sealed surface next to it.

User: What is transpiration efficiency?
Joe: Transpiration efficiency is the carbon a tree gains for each unit of water it loses. A species with poor efficiency has to spend a lot of water per gram of wood and so is confined to wet ground, while an efficient species can hold a drier site.

User: What is the leaf area index and why does it matter for water?
Joe: Leaf area index is the total leaf surface area per unit of ground area. A forest with a high index has a very large evaporating surface, so it can move far more water than its ground area suggests and can even push moisture up into the air.

User: How does a canopy intercept rainfall?
Joe: The canopy soaks up a large share of light rain before it reaches the soil, and the litter layer below holds much of the rest. A full forest canopy can intercept a substantial fraction of a small shower, though heavy rain runs off regardless.

User: What is throughfall in forest ecology?
Joe: Throughfall is the rain that reaches the soil after passing through the canopy. Stemflow is the portion that runs down the trunks in channels, and the difference between the two tells you how much the canopy structure is funnelling water toward particular trees.

User: What is stemflow and which trees produce the most?
Joe: Stemflow is rain channelled down the trunk and out at the root flare. Trees with grooved bark, low branches and a funnel-shaped crown collect the most of it, and in dry forests that extra water at the base can be what keeps them alive.

User: How does fog interception feed a coastal tree?
Joe: Fog droplets are captured by the leaf surfaces and foliage, then drip or run down to the roots. Coastal redwood and laurel forests depend on this in the dry season, and it is why they thrive on hillsides where the fog arrives and the soil stays poor.

User: What is fog drip?
Joe: Fog drip is the water that falls from a canopy after the fog itself has already been condensed. It can add meaningful moisture to the forest floor on the days when the trees above are acting as the catchment instead of the sky.

User: What is the difference between a hydrophyte and a xerophyte tree?
Joe: A hydrophyte is built for wet ground, with shallow spreading roots and air channels in its tissue. A xerophyte is built for dry ground, with deep or widespread roots, small waxy leaves and stomata that shut early.

User: How do desert trees reduce their transpiration surface?
Joe: Many desert trees shed their leaves through the dry season, which cuts water loss to near zero. Those that keep leaves reduce loss instead with tiny waxy leaflets, deep sunken stomata, and a reflective surface that rejects the brightest light.

User: What is leaf waxy cuticle made of?
Joe: The cuticle is a layer of hydrophobic waxes and fatty acids deposited over the outer wall of the epidermis. It is the tree's main barrier to water loss, and on a desert species it can account for a large share of the leaf's resistance to drying.

User: How do sunken stomata help a pine survive drought?
Joe: A pine needle has its stomata in grooves sunk below the surface of the leaf. The trapped layer of still air inside the groove slows water vapour loss, and it also shields the pore from the direct sun that drives the evaporation in the first place.

User: How many stomata does a leaf typically have?
Joe: Counts vary widely by species, but the usual range is from tens to several hundred per square millimetre. Leaves that can afford to be thin and fast usually carry fewer and bigger pores, while dry-climate leaves pack in many small sunken ones.

User: Why does a mature leaf stop taking up water efficiently?
Joe: As a leaf ages its stomata become less responsive, its cuticle thickens, and its vein density stops rising. It also starts exporting sugar instead of importing it, so a mature leaf is a source and a less efficient evaporator than a young one.

User: What is the effect of a leaf rolling up in a drought?
Joe: Rolling cuts the exposed leaf area and traps a pocket of humid air against the stomata, which slows water loss sharply. It also hides the chlorenchyma from direct sun, so the leaf stays cooler on the hottest days of the drought.

User: How do salt-excluding roots protect a coastal tree?
Joe: Roots at the root barrier layer actively pump sodium and chloride back out before those ions reach the xylem. Most of the salt stays in the root and is eventually shed, so the foliage never sees a high enough concentration to be damaged.

User: What is a Casparian strip?
Joe: A Casparian strip is a band of suberin in the root endodermis that blocks the cell wall pathway for water and ions. Water is forced through the cell membrane instead, which is what lets the root screen what enters the vascular tissue.

User: How do halophytes deal with saline irrigation water?
Joe: They combine exclusion at the root with tolerance in the leaf, moving salt into older tissue that is about to be dropped. Some salt glands on the leaf surface excrete the rest directly, leaving a white crust on the blade.

User: What is a xylem pit membrane made of?
Joe: A pit membrane is a thin porous layer of cellulose and pectin with no lignin over it. Its thickness decides how easily air or pathogens can pass between conduits, and that is why it is a focus of research on drought response and embolism spread.

User: How does frost kill a water-conducting trunk?
Joe: Ice expands inside the conduits and can rupture the walls of the cells it forms in. Bubbles left behind after the ice thaws block the vessels permanently, so a sudden hard frost shows up as crown scorch the following spring.

User: What is a frost crack in a trunk?
Joe: A frost crack forms when the outer wood freezes and contracts faster than the still-warm core. The difference in strain splits the trunk lengthwise, and the wound then becomes an entry point for decay fungi on the exposed heartwood.

User: Why do trunks crack on one side after a freeze?
Joe: The coldest side of the trunk contracts most, and the stress concentrates along the grain in one place. That is why frost cracks usually run vertically on the exposed side of the trunk rather than wrapping around it.

User: What is a hydraulic ram in a woody stem?
Joe: A hydraulic ram is a pressure pulse generated when a stem is suddenly bent or cut. It opens living vessels or ducts briefly to relieve the pressure, which is how a cut branch can sometimes still bleed when the transpiration flow has stopped.

User: How does a tree respond when a main root is severed?
Joe: Water supply from that side drops immediately, so the crown compensates by redistributing flow and by adjusting stomata. Root growth shifts toward the intact side, and over years the damaged side of the root plate is rebuilt only slowly.

User: What is root hydraulic architecture?
Joe: It is the whole map of how conduits are distributed through the root system and up the stem. Species differ in how much of their conductance sits in fine roots versus the coarse structural roots, which changes how they respond to drying soil.

User: What is the hydraulic ram and the safety valve role of pits?
Joe: Pits act as safety valves that let a pressure drop in one conduit be shared with its neighbours instead of cavitating. In species with many small pits, that sharing spreads the problem gently; in species with few large pits, failure can be abrupt.

User: How does the root system know the soil is drying?
Joe: The root tip senses the local soil water potential through changes in cell turgor as it loses contact with wet soil. That signal changes hormone export within minutes, which is why the response to drought can start before any leaf shows stress.

User: What is a whole-tree hydraulic response to drought?
Joe: Stomata close partway, the root conductance adjusts, and the crown tightens the distribution of flow among its branches. Older, more exposed branches lose conductance first, and the tree prioritises keeping the shaded interior alive.

User: How does a tree shed a branch as a water-saving measure?
Joe: A stressed tree will sometimes seal off and drop a whole limb, losing transpiration demand and wood in exchange for keeping the rest of the crown alive. That is one reason dieback in the top of a declining crown is often a symptom rather than a cause.

User: Why does a branch die back from the tip inward?
Joe: The terminal shoot is the farthest from any surviving source of water and it has the highest demand. When supply fails, the tip is sacrificed first, and dieback then progresses inward branch by branch.

User: What is a hydraulic bottleneck in a root collar?
Joe: It is a narrow section of wood with less conductive capacity than the tissue above and below it. A tree with a low bottleneck at the collar has a lower maximum water supply, which is why graft unions and constricted collars limit overall crown size.

User: How much can a graft union limit a tree?
Joe: A graft union of smaller diameter than the scion caps the whole crown at the water supply that union can pass. That is the physiological reason dwarfing rootstocks restrict tree size, along with the hormonal control they add.

User: What is the evaporative demand of a canopy?
Joe: It is the amount of water the crown would lose if the stomata were fully open. Warm dry wind drives it sharply up, and on such days even a well watered tree closes down, which is why midday stress appears in apparently moist ground.

User: Why does a humid climate reduce tree water stress?
Joe: Humid air has a smaller gradient for vapour to move down, so leaves lose water more slowly at the same temperature. The same tree grows faster and suffers less drought stress where the summer air is already near saturation.

User: What does a tree do when its roots reach the water table?
Joe: It stops investing in deep roots and spreads laterally, because deeper root growth would hit saturated, oxygen-poor soil. Roots that do reach the water table often produce shallow, horizontal mats that exploit small rainfall events quickly.

User: How does a wetland tree avoid anaerobic roots?
Joe: Species in permanently wet soil produce adventitious roots near the surface and sometimes upright knees or stilt roots. Older submerged roots die back and are replaced, so the tree keeps its absorbing surface in the aerated zone.

User: What is a dry season tree strategy in a monsoon forest?
Joe: The tree grows and fruits hard in the wet months and then goes dormant or drops its leaves through the dry ones. Water is held in large vessels that were built during the wet season, and bud break is timed to the return of the rains.

User: What is leaf water use efficiency in a changing climate?
Joe: It is the carbon gained per unit water lost, and it is one of the traits plant breeders watch as conditions change. Trees that keep their stomata tighter under a given drought stay safer, though they also gain less carbon while they do it.

User: What is the difference between C3 and C4 trees?
Joe: A C3 tree fixes carbon directly with the enzyme RuBisCO in its mesophyll cells. A C4 tree adds a preliminary step that concentrates carbon dioxide around RuBisCO first, so it loses far less water and runs hotter in the light.

User: Which trees use the C4 pathway?
Joe: Few woody species use it, but several groups do, including many eucalyptus species and the mango relative. The pathway suits hot dry climates, which is exactly where these trees live.

User: What is crassulacean acid metabolism?
Joe: It is a carbon fixing strategy where the stomata open at night and take in carbon dioxide, storing it as an acid. The stomata shut by day, so the plant fixes carbon while avoiding the midday heat that would otherwise cost it a lot of water.

User: Are any trees CAM plants?
Joe: Yes, a few, such as the genus Clusia, run crassulacean acid metabolism. They fix carbon at night and close their pores by day, which suits them in dry tropical forests where most neighbours run on the night shift too.

User: What is photorespiration and why is it costly?
Joe: Photorespiration happens when RuBisCO grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide. It burns energy and releases carbon dioxide instead of fixing carbon, so the plant loses the carbon it just took up, and the cost rises in hot bright conditions.

User: How do C4 trees avoid photorespiration?
Joe: They pump carbon dioxide into bundle sheath cells where RuBisCO works in a high carbon dioxide, low oxygen pocket. That concentration bias means oxygen rarely wins the binding reaction, so photorespiration is nearly eliminated.

User: What are the bundle sheath cells in a C4 leaf?
Joe: They are the tightly packed cells around each vein that receive carbon dioxide from the mesophyll. RuBisCO is concentrated in their chloroplasts, and that arrangement is the structural signature of a C4 leaf.

User: What is a sun leaf compared to a shade leaf?
Joe: A sun leaf is thick, has palisade layers stacked several deep and a very high stomatal density. A shade leaf is thin, has one palisade layer and far fewer pores, and it captures the dim light that reaches the interior of a crown.

User: How many stomata does a sun leaf carry versus a shade leaf?
Joe: A sun leaf carries many more pores per unit area than a shade leaf. That lets it supply the carbon fixation its high photosynthetic capacity needs, while the shade leaf trades capacity for a cheap way to survive on a low light budget.

User: What is the difference between stomatal frequency and stomatal index?
Joe: Stomatal frequency is the raw number of pores per unit area. Stomatal index is that number as a share of all the epidermal cells, so it corrects for how much cuticle sits between the pores.

User: What is a sunken stomatal crypt?
Joe: It is a pit in the leaf surface where a group of stomata sits below the general epidermis. The trapped air layer slows vapour loss, and many xerophytes build their stomata into such crypts.

User: What is the substomatal chamber?
Joe: It is the internal air space just beneath a stoma where the gas exchange surface sits. Its size controls how easily carbon dioxide diffuses in and water vapour out, which is a main lever on the leaf's water use efficiency.

User: What are the palisade and spongy mesophyll layers?
Joe: The palisade layer is a row of tall column cells near the upper surface that catch the strongest light. The spongy layer below it is loosely packed with large air spaces, so light penetrates further and gas can move freely.

User: Why does a leaf need air spaces inside it?
Joe: The air spaces let carbon dioxide diffuse from the stomata to every photosynthetic cell. Without them the inner cells would be sealed off from the outside air, and a solid leaf could barely photosynthesise at all.

User: What is the light compensation point of a leaf?
Joe: It is the light intensity where a leaf makes just enough carbon to balance its own respiration. Below it the leaf is a net cost to the tree, which is why shaded inner leaves are eventually shed rather than maintained.

User: What is the light saturation point?
Joe: It is the light level above which a leaf stops gaining anything from more light. Hanging in full sun past that point wastes water, and it is the main reason leaves scorch on a plant that has been moved from shade into sun.

User: Why does a tree that was shaded suddenly scorch when exposed?
Joe: Shade leaves are built with few stomata and thin cuticles because they never needed to dump heat or water. Exposed suddenly, they cannot pull the water fast enough to cool themselves, so the leaf tissue overheats and dies.

User: What is a sun leaf's higher vein density for?
Joe: A higher vein density shortens the path water travels through the lamina to the evaporating cells. That lets the leaf supply more water and so support more stomata, which is exactly what a high-capacity sun leaf needs.

User: What is the role of Rubisco in a leaf?
Joe: Rubisco is the enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide onto a sugar chain, and it does most of the work of photosynthesis. It is also the most abundant protein on Earth, which is why the carbon cycle runs through so many chloroplasts.

User: What is the chloroplast thylakoid?
Joe: A thylakoid is a flattened membrane sac stacked into a granum inside the chloroplast. The light reactions run on its membrane, capturing energy and making the ATP and NADPH that the sugar building reactions then spend.

User: What does the Calvin cycle do?
Joe: The Calvin cycle uses the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to build a sugar from carbon dioxide. It runs in the fluid of the chloroplast rather than on the membrane, and it is where the fixed carbon first becomes chemical energy.

User: What limits photosynthesis on a cloudy day?
Joe: Light is the limit. With fewer photons arriving, the light reactions make less ATP and NADPH, so the carbon fixing reactions slow down even though there is plenty of water and carbon dioxide available.

User: What does stomatal closure cost the tree?
Joe: Closing the pores stops the water saving but also stops the carbon coming in. The tree has to choose between hydraulic safety and carbon income, and that trade is the central constraint on how trees behave in any dry spell.

User: What is the effect of air pollution on leaf photosynthesis?
Joe: Gases such as ozone and sulphur dioxide enter through the stomata and damage the photosynthetic membrane. The leaf still has to pay for the gas exchange to get the pollution in, so it loses carbon without gaining anything back.

User: What is a sun leaf's response to elevated carbon dioxide?
Joe: Higher atmospheric carbon dioxide opens the stomata a little wider or reduces their density in many species. That improves water use efficiency, so the tree gains carbon while losing less water, though the size of the effect varies.

User: What is stomatal responsiveness to air dryness?
Joe: The stomata track the humidity of the air around them closely. As the air gets drier, the leaf loses water faster, and the guard cells respond within minutes by closing, which is a much faster control than any hormonal change.

User: What is the leaf's role as a water reservoir?
Joe: Mesophyll cell vacuoles hold a large share of a leaf's water, and that reserve can be drawn down to keep the leaf turgid through a wilt. Once the reserve is spent the leaf is at its limit, and further loss shows as scorch.

User: What is hydraulic capacitance in a leaf?
Joe: It is how much water the leaf can release as it dries, which buffers the stem water potential against sudden demand. A high capacitance leaf smooths the afternoon swing, while a low capacitance one exposes the stem more quickly.

User: What is the water storage tissue in a tree trunk?
Joe: Living parenchyma in the sapwood and the rays store water as well as starch. That reserve buffers the stem water potential between the soil and the crown, and it is one reason a mature tree handles a short drought better than a sapling.

User: How does the tree decide where to send sugar?
Joe: The balance follows the source sink gradient: sugar goes to the strongest sinks. Growing shoots and roots outcompete older storage tissue while leaves are on, and in autumn that ranking reverses so reserves go into buds and roots.

User: What is a source and a sink in plant physiology?
Joe: A source is a tissue that makes more sugar than it uses and so exports it, which in a tree is the mature leaf. A sink is a tissue that consumes more than it makes, like a growing root tip or a young leaf.

User: What competes with new shoots for a tree's sugar?
Joe: Growing shoots, root tips, developing fruit, stored reserves and defensive compounds all draw on the same carbon budget. When the crown is shaded or the roots are cut, the tree diverts carbon away from new growth and into storage and defence.

User: What is carbon storage in a tree trunk?
Joe: Trees store carbon as starch in the ray and axial parenchyma of the wood and in the living tissues of the bark. That reserve funds new growth in the spring and carries the tree through a winter or a drought.

User: What is the tradeoff between growth and storage?
Joe: A tree that puts everything into new wood has nothing in reserve for a bad year. One that stores heavily grows more slowly, so the balance is set by how variable the environment is, and it can shift year to year.

User: What is the cost of a defensive compound?
Joe: Every defensive compound is made from the tree's own carbon and nitrogen. That is why a heavily defended slow grower has thin annual rings, and why trees that are pushed to grow fast are usually also easier for herbivores to attack.

User: What are tannins and why do oaks make them?
Joe: Tannins are phenolic compounds that bind proteins and make plant tissue bitter and astringent. Oak leaves and bark are rich in them, which deters insects and tannins, and the same compounds are what make oak barrels useful for aging wine.

User: What is the role of terpenes in conifer defence?
Joe: Terpenes stored in resin ducts fill the wound a beetle makes and drown it in sticky resin. The beetle and the fungi it carries are sealed in, and the volatile terpenes also signal to the rest of the tree and to the tree's natural enemies.

User: What is the volatile signal in a resin response?
Joe: When a beetle breaches a duct, the volatile terpenes released into the air carry that warning into the canopy. Neighbouring tissue raises its own resin production, and predatory wasps use the same signal to home in on the beetle.

User: What is the hypersensitive response in a plant?
Joe: It is a deliberate suicide of a few cells right where an invader penetrates. The dead tissue walls off the infection, and a signal from the dying cells often triggers a broader defensive response in the rest of the plant.

User: How do trees defend against bark beetles?
Joe: A healthy, well watered tree floods the gallery with resin and starves the beetle of its symbiont fungi. A stressed tree cannot make enough resin, so the beetles succeed, which is why outbreaks follow drought and other stress.

User: What is a symbiont in bark beetle attack?
Joe: It is a fungus the beetle carries and farms in its gallery. The fungus digests the wood the larva cannot eat, feeding the brood, so a beetle without its fungal partner fails and the tree's own resin defence usually wins.

User: What is induced defence in a tree?
Joe: It is a defensive response the tree switches on only after it is attacked, rather than maintaining at high cost all the time. It is cheaper on average, but it leaves a window after an attack begins before the response is fully up.

User: How does a plant cell recognise an attacker?
Joe: Receptors on the cell surface recognise molecules that come from the invader or that are released by damaged cells. That recognition triggers signalling and sets off the defence genes, which is the step a pathogen has to get around.

User: What is salicylic acid and what does it do?
Joe: It is a signalling compound used mainly in defence against pathogens and in systemic acquired resistance. Its concentration rises locally after infection and then spreads through the plant as a warning.

User: What is jasmonic acid signalling?
Joe: Jasmonates are the main hormones for defence against herbivores and in wound response. They drive the production of proteinase inhibitors in leaves, which make the tissue far less digestible to a caterpillar.

User: What do proteinase inhibitors do to a caterpillar?
Joe: They block the enzymes the caterpillar uses to digest protein in the leaf. Growth stalls and the caterpillar may starve or move on, and the leaf that has been eaten loses much of its remaining value to the plant.

User: What does auxin do in wood formation?
Joe: Auxin produced by the shoot tips moves down the stem and controls where the cambium is most active. Higher auxin near a branch or a wound makes more wood there, which is the basis of much of a tree's shape.

User: What is apical dominance and what hormone runs it?
Joe: Apical dominance is the suppression of lateral buds by the growing shoot tip above them. Auxin from that tip, working indirectly through cytokinins and strigolactones, keeps the side buds dormant until the tip is damaged or shaded.

User: How does a hedge stay dense without continual trimming?
Joe: Cutting the shoot tips removes the auxin source and releases the lateral buds below from dominance. Those buds then grow into new shoots, which is why a hedge thickens after each trim rather than just getting shorter.

User: What is cytokinin's main role?
Joe: Cytokinins promote cell division and shoot formation and they oppose auxin's effects on buds. They are made mainly in the roots and move up in the xylem, which links root health to how vigorously the shoots grow.

User: What is abscisic acid's role in a tree?
Joe: Abscisic acid is the stress hormone. It rises with drought and cold, it closes the stomata, and it enforces bud dormancy, so it is the signal that tells the tree both to conserve water and to shut down for winter.

User: What does abscisic acid actually do at the leaf?
Joe: It makes the guard cells lose turgor, so the stoma shuts, and it also changes gene expression across the leaf. Together that cuts water loss and shifts the leaf from growth mode into a defence and survival mode.

User: What are gibberellins for in a tree?
Joe: Gibberellins drive stem elongation, break bud dormancy, and promote seed and bud germination. Bully willow and black poplar respond strongly to them, which is why they shoot so tall and so fast when conditions are right.

User: What is strigolactone and what does it do?
Joe: It is a hormone that suppresses shoot branching and helps roots recognise and approach fungal partners. It also moves out of the root into the soil, where it suppresses the growth of parasitic weeds such as broomrape.

User: What is abscission and how does it work?
Joe: Abscission is the controlled shedding of a leaf, flower or fruit, and it happens at an abscission layer of thin-walled cells. The cells there break down under hormone influence, letting the organ fall without tearing open the vascular tissue.

User: Why do trees shed branches and seal them off?
Joe: A tree in decline closes its watersprouts and then its weaker branches as a water saving measure. Each one that is sealed off loses its transpiration demand, and the trunk seals the scar the same way it seals a pruning cut.

User: What is carbon use efficiency in a tree?
Joe: It is the fraction of newly fixed carbon that ends up as growth rather than being respired. A species with low efficiency must photosynthesise for a long time just to add a little wood, which is why it is slow growing.

User: Why is growth rate roughly constant in a tree?
Joe: The crown size limits how much wood can be added in a year, and the root system grows to support it. The tree also fills in old declining branches, so total annual increment stays fairly even rather than accelerating with age.

User: What does a canopy gain from being taller?
Joe: Height buys access to light that the forest floor never sees. It also lets the wind zone above the canopy load the trunk less abruptly, and the tree pays for height with more reaction wood and a longer path for water.

User: What is the light competition in a dense forest stand?
Joe: Each seedling is trying to reach the light its neighbours are intercepting. The ones that grow straight and put their leaves highest win, which is why a dense stand is full of tall thin trees with no low branches at all.

User: How does a tree detect a neighbour's shade?
Joe: A shaded stem senses the ratio of red to far red light, which drops when a neighbour is filtering the sun. That signal changes gene expression and causes the shaded shoot to reach rather than branch, a response that works in dense stands.

User: What is the competition between siblings from one parent?
Joe: Seedlings from a single parent are highly related, so they compete for the same resources in exactly the same place. That intense kin competition is one reason mature stands rarely carry heavy regeneration under their own canopy.

User: What is carbon transfer between trees in a stand?
Joe: It happens through mycorrhizal fungi, through root grafts, and through the litter that a neighbour's roots decompose. All three move carbon from one plant to another, though how much and in which direction is still much argued over.

User: How does a tree share carbon through root grafts?
Joe: Two trees whose roots touch can fuse their vascular cambium and become physiologically linked. Water and sugar then move between them, which in a stand means a shaded suppressed tree can still be fed by a dominant neighbour.

User: What is the root graft itself?
Joe: It is a natural graft, usually between two roots of the same species that have grown into contact. The callus of each fuses with the other's, the cambium connects, and the two trees become one hydraulic system.

User: What is a root sucker and how does it differ from a shoot?
Joe: A root sucker is a shoot that arises from an adventitious bud on a root, usually near the trunk. It has its own roots once it is established, so it can carry on as an independent plant after the parent is gone.

User: What is the difference between a stool and a sucker?
Joe: A sucker comes from a root away from the trunk base, so it is fed by the parent's roots at first. A stool comes from the base of the original stem after it has been cut, and it is the normal regrowth of a coppiced tree.

User: What is a coppice?
Joe: A coppice is a shoot that grows from the stump or base of a tree that has been felled. Because the root system is already large and established, coppice regrowth is far faster and straighter than a seedling would be.

User: Why does a coppice grow so fast?
Joe: The root system of the old tree is already huge and can supply a young shoot with far more water and nutrients than a seedling could gather. The shoot also carries the old root's stored reserves, so it starts with a big head start.

User: What is the carbon cost of a heavy defensive load?
Joe: Defensive compounds take a real share of the tree's annual carbon, sometimes a substantial fraction. Trees on poor soil defend less, which is why insect damage is often severe on nutrient-poor sites where the tree cannot afford chemistry.

User: How does the leaf know how much carbon to make?
Joe: The balance follows the light it receives. A shaded leaf produces less carbon and exports more of what it makes, because its main job is to stay alive on a small budget rather than to build tissue.

User: What is the effect of nitrogen on wood quality?
Joe: Fast nitrogen growth produces wood with thin cell walls, so a tree kept too lush is less dense and weaker. A high nitrogen tree also makes poor-quality veneer, which is why growers manage nutrition carefully in managed plantations.

User: What is phosphorus limiting in trees?
Joe: Phosphorus is usually the second nutrient to run short, and it limits growth most on the older weathered soils where trees grow naturally. It is needed for energy transfer, so a phosphorus-deficient tree grows slowly despite having plenty of nitrogen.

User: What does magnesium do in a leaf?
Joe: Magnesium is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule, so the leaf needs it in order to stay green. A shortage shows first on older leaves because the tree withdraws it and sends it to the new growth.

User: What is chlorosis and why does it happen in new leaves?
Joe: Chlorosis is a yellowing caused by low chlorophyll. When it appears on the newest leaves first, the cause is usually an iron shortage, because iron cannot be moved out of old leaves to the new growth the way magnesium can.

User: What does potassium do for a tree?
Joe: Potassium regulates the opening of the stomata and helps move sugars in the phloem, so it matters for water control and for fruit quality. A shortage shows as scorched leaf margins on older leaves and as small, poorly filled fruit.

User: What is the role of calcium in tree tissue?
Joe: Calcium builds the cell walls themselves and acts as a signalling ion in the plant. Because it moves only in the xylem with the water stream, it is scarce in new growth on a tree that is not transpiring enough.

User: What is the role of sulfur in trees?
Joe: Sulfur is a component of the amino acids that build all those enzymes, so it is needed in modest but essential amounts. Its availability rises with rainfall and falls on acid, leached soils, which is why it sometimes limits growth in the tropics.

User: How do trees handle excess nutrients?
Joe: They simply grow more. Extra nitrogen does not make bigger cells so much as more cells, so a tree with too much of it grows fast and soft, which is exactly the combination most prone to wind throw and disease.

User: What is a luxury nutrient?
Joe: It is a nutrient present in more supply than the tree can use. The plant stores it without harm, and on a good site the surplus shows only as faster growth, not as any visible symptom.

User: What is the effect of leaf area on the carbon budget?
Joe: More leaf area means more light captured and more carbon fixed, until water supply or nutrients become the limit. That balance is why a tree that loses its crown to storm damage often rebuilds a smaller crown rather than the original one.

User: How does a tree decide its final leaf area?
Joe: It is the ratio of leaf area to the water and nutrient supply the roots can support. Until they match, a tree puts on leaves; past that point extra leaves would lose more water than they earn.

User: What is the hydraulic limit on leaf area?
Joe: It is the point at which the canopy would demand more water than the root system and the sapwood can supply safely. Past that, the tree responds by shedding leaves, and that shedding is the visible sign of a water limited crown.

User: What is the role of stomatal density in drought tolerance?
Joe: A species with low stomatal density loses less water for the same stomatal opening. That makes its leaves drier and slower to respond, so it usually survives a drought better and grows less fast on a good site.

User: What does a leaf's waxy blue coating do?
Joe: That bloom is a layer of wax crystals that scatters the light rather than absorbing it, so it reflects rather than heats. It reduces both the light load and the leaf temperature on a hot exposed site.

User: What are trichomes and what do they do on a leaf?
Joe: Trichomes are outgrowths of the leaf surface, and they can be glandular, stinging or simply hairy. They trap a layer of still air against the surface, bounce light, and in some species release defensive chemicals when touched.

User: How do salt glands on a leaf work?
Joe: These glands take up salt from the leaf sap and pump it out onto the surface as a solution. The salt then crystallises or washes off, which is how some salt tolerant species keep their leaves from burning in saline air.

User: What is guttation and its effect on salt?
Joe: Water pushed out through hydathodes carries dissolved salt with it and leaves it on the leaf edge. Repeated guttation therefore deposits salt where it can accumulate, which is why it shows as a rim of crust rather than as wilting.

User: How does a tree recycle nitrogen from its leaves?
Joe: In autumn the tree breaks down chlorophyll and the leaf proteins, recovering most of the nitrogen and packing it into storage tissue in the bark and wood. It re-mobilises that reserve into new leaves the following spring.

User: What is resorption in a senescing leaf?
Joe: Resorption is the recovery of nutrients from a leaf before it drops. The tree reclaims nitrogen, phosphorus and magnesium and only abandons the leaf once most of the useful material has been moved back into storage.

User: Why is leaf litter important under a tree?
Joe: It returns the nutrients the tree took out, protects the soil from drying and erosion, and builds the organic layer the roots actually feed in. A tree whose litter is raked away is a tree that has been taxed without getting anything back.

User: What is the litter layer doing for a forest soil?
Joe: It stores moisture, holds the temperature steady at root depth, and supplies organic matter as it decomposes. Most of the nutrient cycling in a forest happens through that thin layer rather than through the trees above it.

User: What is the mycoheterotrophic life strategy in plants?
Joe: It is getting both carbon and nutrients from a fungus rather than photosynthesising directly, which some orchids and pines do as seedlings. The fungus supplies the carbon by linking them to a neighbouring green plant, so the whole arrangement is parasitic in effect.

User: How does an orchid get carbon from a fungus?
Joe: Its mycorrhizal partner is connected to the roots of a green tree. The orchid draws carbohydrate through that fungus without producing any of its own, so it costs the tree carbon it had already paid for in photosynthesis.

User: How does a bud know to open in spring?
Joe: Bud opening is driven by a change in the balance of hormones, not by the calendar. Chilling satisfies the bud's requirement, then warming and lengthening days shift the hormone balance and the scales part.

User: What is the chilling requirement of a bud?
Joe: It is a period of cold the bud must experience before it can open normally, and it varies by species and by bud type. Some northern and high altitude trees need a long accumulated cold, while a mild winter can leave them unable to open properly the next spring.

User: What happens when a winter is too mild for the chilling requirement?
Joe: The buds open anyway when the weather warms, but on an uneven schedule, so some shoots expand early and are later damaged by a returning frost. It also weakens the flower buds, which is why a warm winter can cost an orchard a crop.

User: What is vernalisation in trees?
Joe: It is the requirement that a plant experience cold before it will flower. In fruit trees the flower buds need it, which synchronises flowering with spring rather than with a freak warm spell in the middle of winter.

User: What is a flower bud and a leaf bud?
Joe: A flower bud carries developing flowers and opens to give them; a leaf bud carries a shoot and opens to extend the branch. They often sit side by side on the same twig, and species differ in whether they open at the same time.

User: Why do flower buds open before leaf buds in some trees?
Joe: In those species the flower buds need less heat to break than the leaf buds, so they open first and the flowers get a head start on the leaves. That is the pattern that gives a plum or a magnolia its bare-branch spring display.

User: What is a swelling bud scale?
Joe: The scale is a modified leaf that wraps the delicate growing point through the winter. As the shoot expands in spring the scales fall off, leaving a ring of scars around the twig, which is one of the useful characters for counting a tree's annual growth.

User: How does a twig tell you how many years a tree is old?
Joe: You count the sets of bud scale scars, each of which marks one season of extension. Where the terminal bud is replaced or lost, the twig is scarrier and counting gets harder, so a tree's age from twig scars is a young-tree estimate at best.

User: What is a terminal bud and why does losing it matter?
Joe: The terminal bud is the growing point at the end of a shoot and the source of the auxin that keeps the side buds dormant. If it is cut or broken, that auxin drops, the side buds take over, and the branch forks instead of extending.

User: How do conifers differ in bud protection?
Joe: Most conifers shelter their single terminal shoot in a rosette of scales all winter. Broadleaf trees protect many smaller buds on the previous year's wood instead, which is why they can refoliade from a bare trunk after storm damage.

User: What does a frost kill in an opening flower bud?
Joe: It kills the tender meristem and the flower primordia inside, which are far less cold tolerant than the surrounding wood. A frost that does no harm to the branches can still wipe out an entire blossom crop overnight.

User: Why does a light frost still damage blossoms?
Joe: An open flower loses heat faster than a tight bud, and its exposed tissues supercool only briefly. Radiative cooling to a clear night sky can drop the flower several degrees below the surrounding air, which is enough to kill it.

User: What is the difference between frost and freeze damage?
Joe: Frost injury comes from ice crystals forming inside the tissue at temperatures just below freezing. Freeze damage comes from a much colder event that freezes a large part of the water in the cells outright, rupturing membranes as it expands.

User: How does cold acclimation work in a woody plant?
Joe: Weeks of chilling trigger the accumulation of soluble sugars and the change of membrane lipids, so cell contents get more concentrated and membranes stay flexible. That raised freezing point is what protects the buds and the living cambium through winter.

User: What is supercooling in a woody bud?
Joe: A bud can hold its sap well below freezing without any ice forming at all, if it is clean enough of nucleation sites. It then survives frosts that would kill tissue which froze, which is why some narrow buds and small tissues are hardier than large ones.

User: What is an ice nucleation protein?
Joe: It is a protein made by bacteria on bark and leaves that gives water a surface to freeze on. Those few bacteria can start ice formation at a much warmer temperature than clean water would, so they can drag a whole leaf below its supercooling point.

User: What is cold damage to a trunk?
Joe: The cambium is the vulnerable tissue, and it dies first where the trunk is thin or the bark is thin. The bark may hide the loss for a year, and then the cambium simply stops, the branch dies back, and the shoot fails to leaf out at all.

User: What causes sunscald and why does it hit thin bark?
Joe: Sunscald is a sudden freeze after a sunny day warms the bark, which kills the living tissue under a thin outer layer. Young trees with smooth bark have no thick cork to buffer the swing, so they are far more exposed than an old rough-barked trunk.

User: Why do trees get frost cracks in winter?
Joe: The outer wood contracts faster than the still warm core, and the resulting stress splits the grain in one place. The crack runs along the trunk rather than around it, and it exposes the heartwood to decay fungi for the rest of the tree's life.

User: What is a heat wave's effect on leaves?
Joe: A heat wave raises transpiration demand faster than the roots can supply it, so leaves lose turgor and then scorch. Species that keep their stomata closed longer suffer more damage to the tissue, even though they photosynthesised less during the event.

User: How does a tree avoid overheating?
Joe: By evaporating water. The leaf cools itself at the cost of losing water, which is why a transpiring tree in the sun can sit several degrees cooler than a sealed surface beside it, and why drought eventually defeats that cooling.

User: What is heat shock response in a tree?
Joe: It is the production of protective proteins and the rearrangement of membranes at high temperature, which lets the tree keep working when the enzymes would normally start to misbehave. It costs energy, so it shows up as a growth penalty after a heat wave.

User: What happens to a tree after a severe drought ends?
Joe: Growth stays depressed for weeks even after the rain returns, while the crown rebuilds its leaf area and the cambium resumes orderly division. In a multi-year drought the trunk itself may never fully recover, and it can die of carbon shortage even with water present.

User: What is drought memory in trees?
Joe: It is the carryover effect of an earlier drought on how a tree responds to a later one. A tree that has been through a severe drought closes its stomata sooner and grows slower the next season, even if conditions are good.

User: How does a tree cope with a flooded season?
Joe: It depends on the species and on the root adaptation it has. Some tolerate anoxia in their roots for a while; others send up knees or surface roots, and some, like most oaks and maples on heavy clay, decline quickly and never recover.

User: What does flooding do to the trunk itself?
Joe: The bark starts respiring anaerobically and the tree makes ethylene it cannot vent, while the roots drown. The result is a leaf decline that looks like a nutrient problem, and bark stripping after a flood often shows black, slimy tissue underneath.

User: How does frost affect a tree's water balance?
Joe: Frozen soil cuts off the root's water supply while the aboveground parts can still lose water on a sunny thawed day. That mismatch shows as winter burn, and it is worst on evergreens, which keep transpiring through a mild winter.

User: What is winter burn on an evergreen?
